title: Chapter 202 – Wall Season
html:
[Section Nine of the Great Wall – Han]

Han counts the mules, then counts them again, because the number is wrong.

She stands on the parapet of section nine with her gloved hands on the frozen stone and watches the wagon train come up the pass. Forty wagons, empty, creaking under their canvas. Forty pairs of mules, gray with road dust, blowing steam. Beside them the drivers walk with their heads down against the wind. She counted forty at dawn, when the last one went out of the gate. She has counted forty-one three times now, in the gray light, and the forty-first is not a wagon.

It is a handcart, pulled by a broad slow man in a heavy cloak. On the cart sits a small woman in a patched blue smock with a black kettle in her lap.

"Warden," says the sentry at her elbow. He is a boy of seventeen with a spear too big for him. "Shall I sound the horn?"

"No."

"But there are two strangers—"

"They are not strangers." Han's mouth twists. It is not quite a smile. "They are Lins. And I think, if you value your supper, you will let them in without a fuss."

The boy blinks. She has already turned away, down the stair, toward the gate.

* * *

Wenyuan has aged ten years in a month, and Han does not say so.

He climbs down from the cart in the courtyard under the wall's long shadow, stiffly, one hand on the shaft. His shoulders are broad, but they have lost something. The set of the spine is the same. The cloak is the same, brown wool patched at the hem. But the man inside it moves like one who has been carrying a weight too long and has learned to hide the limp. His eyes find hers across the yard, level and tired, and he inclines his head.

"Keeper," he says.

"Wenyuan." She does not return the title. She has known him too long. "You are early."

"We were told the Wall was short of hands."

"The Wall is always short of hands." She looks past him at the cart, at the small blue shape that has already climbed down and is peering at the courtyard with the frank appraising stare of a woman inspecting a rival's kitchen. "And Madam Qinghe. You have brought your own kettle."

"I did not wish to be a burden."

"You will be a burden," says Han. "You will be the heaviest one I have. Every man on this Wall will eat three bowls and ask for a fourth, and by spring I will have forgotten how to be stern."

Qinghe's face breaks into a slow, delighted smile.

"That," she says, "is exactly what I came for."

* * *

The Wall is an old thing, and tired, and Han loves it with a fierce, stubborn, unsentimental love.

She was born in its shadow. Her mother held section four for thirty years; her grandmother held section nine for thirty more. Her earliest memory is of the cold: a gray winter dawn, a high stone corridor, a spear taller than she was, and a hand on her head. This is the Wall, said the hand. It holds because we do. She has believed it all her life. She believes it still, though she has lately begun to suspect that the sentence leaves something out.

Section nine runs for two miles along a ridge of black rock, from the Gap on the east to the Spur on the west, with a watchtower every quarter mile and a gate in the middle. Below it, to the north, lie the Barrens: a gray waste of stone and snow, empty, silent, the place the beasts came from. Above it, to the south, lies the valley, the Hall, the Garden, the whole warm green world that the Wall exists to keep. It is not a great wall, as walls go. It is only a rampart, thirty feet high and ten thick, built by hands that no one remembers. But it has stood for six hundred years, and Han has spent thirty of them walking its length.

She walks it now, with Wenyuan at her side, in the dusk.

They do not speak for a long while. The wind is bitter. The snow squeaks under their boots. Every few hundred paces a sentry salutes, and she nods, and they go on. The sky is the color of a bruise.

"You have kept it well," says Wenyuan at last.

"Elder Gu has kept it. I have only carried the soup."

"He is still in the keystone?"

"Still." She does not look at the tower ahead, where a faint steady light glows in the topmost window. "Eleven weeks. He sleeps four hours a night, now. The rest he spends in the stone."

"And the beasts?"

"Gone. Every one. They went home a month ago, in the night, all together. I stood on this parapet and watched them go. A hundred thousand, I think. They filed back into the Barrens like a congregation leaving a church." She hesitates. "They sang. I never knew beasts could sing."

"Nor did I."

"Qinghe says it was your son."

"My son would say it was a woman in a white cave," says Wenyuan, dryly. "And that the woman had a mark on her hand."

Han stops.

He stops with her. They stand at the angle of the Wall where it turns south toward the Spur, and the wind howls past the stone like a thing in pain. She turns, slowly, and meets his steady eyes.

"The Veiled," she says.

"Hua."

"You know her name."

"I know a good deal now." He folds his arms. "I have a daughter who hears things, and a son who will not tell me anything. Between them I get most of it."

"And is she to be trusted?"

"She is a mother," says Wenyuan. "And a Lin, and a healer, and the Warden of the Hall. And I do not think she knows which of those she will choose to be." A pause. "But she opened a door for my son when no one else could, and it cost her something. I will give her that."

Han nods slowly. She turns back to the wall.

"The Sect seal," she says. "The mark that was on it. You have heard."

"Jian said."

"There is a man at the gate."

Wenyuan's head comes up.

"He came this morning," says Han. "Before your cart. An Elder of the Azure Cloud Sect, in a gray silk gown, with six disciples behind him and a letter under seal. He asked for the Warden of the Wall. He did not say what for." She lifts her chin. "I put him in the guest hall and told him I would receive him tomorrow. I did not tell him that I already knew what the letter said."

"How?"

"Because I have read the Roll, too." Her mouth is grim. "The Sect has a seal. The seal is the mark on a woman's palm. A woman who has been walking the valley for six hundred years, with no memory, pressing it into wax. They have been using it, Wenyuan. For centuries. They did not know what it opened."

"And now they do."

"Now they have heard it opened something."

* * *

The Elder's name is Ye Shuhan, and he is the smoothest man Han has ever hated.

He receives her in the guest hall at dawn, standing, with his hands tucked into the sleeves of his gray silk gown. He is perhaps sixty, tall and lean, with a face like a polished knife and a thin gray beard trimmed to a point. His six disciples line the wall behind him, as silent as chess pieces. A brazier burns at his feet. A cup of tea sits untasted on the low table beside him.

"Keeper Han," he says. He has a soft, warm voice, a voice for comforting widows. "You are kind to receive me."

"You came a long way."

"Three weeks, through the snow. It is a poor season for travel." He smiles. "But the Sect is anxious to make the acquaintance of its neighbors, now that the beasts have withdrawn. We have been, I fear, rather isolated."

"For six hundred years."

"For six hundred and twelve." He inclines his head. "The Founders' decree. We were to keep to the south side of the mountains and not trouble the Wall. We have kept it faithfully. But we have also, of late, begun to feel that the decree was made for a different age."

Han folds her arms.

"What age?"

"One in which the Wall was necessary." He lifts a finger, gently. "The beasts are gone. The Wall stands, but it guards an empty waste. And we in the Sect have begun to wonder, Keeper, whether the time has not come to speak plainly about what lies behind it."

"Behind it."

"In the valley. In the Hall." The soft voice does not change. "We have heard rumors, Keeper. We have heard of a Warden who is not a Warden. A tree that sings. A stair that goes down for seven hundred steps. A woman with a mark on her hand." He draws a folded paper from his sleeve. "We have a seal, you see. We have always had it. We were told it was a memento of the Founders, a token of their favor. We did not know it was a key."

"And now you do."

"Now we hope to be told by the one who holds the door." He extends the paper. "This is a formal request, on the Sect Master's authority. We wish to send an embassy to the Hall of the Sixth Door. Twelve Elders. A hundred disciples. In the spirit of friendship, to see what our ancestors guarded, and to offer our assistance with its stewardship."

Han does not take the paper.

"The Hall has a covenant," she says.

"Has it?"

"Nobody sleeps or wakes who does not choose it. Nobody is taken. Nobody is kept." She keeps her voice flat. "It was written by a girl of fourteen and read aloud in front of four hundred people. I am told it was well received."

"How charming."

"It is not a charm. It is the law."

"Whose law?"

"The Nine's."

For the first time something moves behind the smooth face. It is small and quick, like a fish turning in deep water. "The Nine," repeats Ye Shuhan. "There were nine, once. They are long gone."

"There are nine now."

"Children, I am told."

"Yes."

"How remarkable." He tucks the paper back in his sleeve. "Then I must hope they are very wise children. Because the Sect is rather old, Keeper, and rather large, and has been patient for a very long time."

* * *

Qinghe takes over the Keeper's kitchen that afternoon, and the Wall has never been so loud.

Han hears it from the courtyard: the clatter of pots, the slap of dough on a board, the sharp warm voice calling for onions. A line has already formed at the door, guards in their gray quilted gowns, shuffling and sniffing the air like hounds. A boy of ten with a bucket is being sent to the well for the third time. Two old soldiers are arguing over who gets to carry the flour.

She puts her head round the door.

Qinghe is standing at the long stove with her sleeves rolled to the elbow, a wooden spoon in her fist and a smudge of flour on her cheek. She is stirring a pot the size of a washtub. Her eyes are half closed. She does not sniff, or taste, or lift the lid. She only stirs, and every so often adds a pinch of something from the pocket of her smock, with the unhurried confidence of a woman who has done this ten thousand times.

"You cannot smell it," says Han, wondering.

"No."

"Then how do you know when it is ready?"

"I listen." Qinghe taps the pot with the spoon. A low round note answers. "A stew speaks when it is done. A little lower than before. It is quite plain, if you pay attention."

"And the salt?"

"My hands remember the salt."

Han looks at the pot, the steam, the wooden spoon moving in a slow figure eight. She has fought for thirty years on a frozen wall and has never, she realizes, been fed with such deliberate care.

"Does it trouble you?" she says. "The loss?"

Qinghe considers. Her spoon does not stop.

"Every morning," she says at last. "For about a minute. And then someone comes in hungry, and I forget."

She tastes nothing, and the soup is perfect. Han eats three bowls, and does not feel the least bit stern.

She tells Elder Gu at dusk, in the tower, with the wind at the shutters.

He is sitting on a stool in the topmost room, as he has sat for eleven weeks, with his bare feet on the cold stone and his hands open on his knees. His eyes are closed. His white hair has grown long and wild; his cheeks have hollowed. There is a pale glow about him, faint and steady, like the light under a door. When she enters it flickers, and he opens his eyes.

"Keeper."

"Elder."

"I heard the Sect's man," he says. His voice is a dry whisper. "In the stone. He has a quiet step, but the Wall hears all things."

"What do you think?"

"I think he wants the key." The old man smiles faintly. "And I think he knows that the key is a woman, and a woman may be persuaded."

"Hua is not for persuading."

"Nor am I." Gu lifts a hand and lets it fall. "But I am a good deal older than the Sect, and I remember what they were. A poor little school at the foot of the mountains. Forty disciples and a bad well. They grew rich on the Founders' scraps." His mouth twists. "They have never forgiven the Founders for being gone."

Han crosses to the window. She stands with her back to him, looking out at the Barrens, the gray plain going blue in the dusk.

"I can refuse the embassy," she says. "I can turn him away at the gate."

"You can."

"But they will come anyway. With armies, or tricks, or letters from the Sect Master. And the Wall will not hold against them, because the Wall was built to face north."

"Yes."

"And you are the keystone."

"I am." He sounds almost cheerful. "And I am dying, Keeper. You know that. I have known since the first week. The stone takes more than it gives."

She does not turn. Her hands, on the sill, are white.

"How long?"

"A month. Perhaps two." The glow about him flickers, steadies. "I did not wish to say. You have had enough to carry."

"You should have told me."

"I am telling you now." His voice is very gentle. "And I am telling you also that you will need another."

"No."

"Han—"

"I will not have it." She spins. Her face is hard, but her eyes are bright. "I will not lose another. I lost Lan Wen. I lost half my guard. I will not stand on this parapet and watch you go dark."

"It is not for you to refuse."

"Then who?"

"Someone who can bear it." The old man closes his eyes. "Someone with a body that does not die of old age. Someone the stone will accept, because the stone has accepted his blood. A Lin."

She stares at him.

"Wenyuan," she says.

"Yes."

"You would ask him to—"

"I would ask no one." Gu smiles again, tiredly. "I am only telling you what the Wall wants. It wants a Lin. It has always wanted one. It was built by Lins, and it keeps Lins, and when the last of them is gone, it will fall." He lifts his hand, and the glow rises, a thread of pale light streaming from his fingers into the stones. "He is already here. I felt him arrive. I have been waiting for him since before you were born."

* * *

That night she walks the parapet alone, and finds the Sect's Elder walking it, too.

He stands at the angle of the Wall, in his gray silk gown, with his hands tucked in his sleeves and his face turned north. A single lantern burns at his feet. He does not hear her until she is nearly upon him, and when he turns there is no start in him at all, only that soft, tolerant smile.

"Keeper. I hope you do not mind. I could not sleep."

"The guest hall has a bed."

"Beds are for the young." He gestures at the Barrens, the pale plain under the stars. "I was thinking how very large it is. A whole country, empty. And you hold it with two miles of stone and a few hundred spears."

"It is enough."

"It has been enough. For six hundred years." He turns the lantern with the toe of his boot. "You know, Keeper, I read the Wall's charter before I came. It is a moving document. It says that the Wall was raised to keep the valley whole. A curious word. Not safe, not free. Whole."

"It means what it says."

"Does it?" He tilts his head. "I wonder what the Founders thought the valley was lacking, to need keeping whole. I wonder what was inside, that might one day want to get out."

Han says nothing. The wind pulls at her cloak.

"Forgive an old man his speculations," says Ye Shuhan, and bows. "I shall be gone by the new moon. But I shall return, Keeper. With my embassy, or without. The Sect has waited six hundred years to see what its ancestors hid. I do not think we shall wait another."

He picks up the lantern, and goes. The little flame bobs away along the parapet, and Han stands in the dark for a long time, with her hand on the cold stone, feeling, for the first time in thirty years, that the Wall is facing the wrong way.

Wenyuan listens to it all without a word.

They sit in the kitchen of the Keeper's house, a low stone room with a hearth and a long scarred table, where Qinghe has already taken possession of the stove. The smell of onions fills the air. A dozen guards sit along the benches, eating, pretending not to listen. Wenyuan sits at the head of the table with his hands folded in front of him and his eyes on the grain of the wood.

"It will cost you," says Han. "I will not lie. Gu has been in the stone for eleven weeks, and it has taken the sight from his left eye and the feeling from both his feet. In the end it will take everything. You will not be able to leave the tower. You will not be able to lift a sword. You will be the Wall."

"For how long?"

"Until a better keystone is found."

"And if none is?"

"Then forever." She cannot soften it. "That is what keystone means."

He is silent. Qinghe has stopped stirring. The only sound in the room is the hiss of the stew.

"My son," says Wenyuan slowly, "is a hundred and nineteen years old and coughing blood. He has given ten years of his life to a child he met a week ago. He has two shaking hands. He has not slept properly since the Night of Counting." His voice is level. "He is fighting for something I do not understand, in a place I have never seen, against enemies I cannot name. And all I can do for him is carry a sword."

"Wenyuan—"

"I have thought about it. All week." He lifts his eyes. "I thought: what is the use of a father who cannot reach his son? And I thought: if I cannot reach him, I can at least guard the road behind him."

"That is not the same."

"No." He smiles, a small tired smile. "But it is something."

Qinghe puts down the spoon. She comes across the room, slowly, wiping her hands on her smock, and stands beside her husband's chair. She does not say anything. She puts her hand on his shoulder. After a long moment he covers it with his own.

"You are a stubborn old fool," she says.

"I have heard."

"You will not be able to hold me."

"I will be able to see you." His voice cracks. "Every morning, from the tower. You will come up with the kettle. I will drink the tea."

"And in the evenings?"

"In the evenings," says Wenyuan, "you will tell me what the boy wrote."

She laughs. It is a cracked wet sound. She bends and kisses the top of his gray head, quickly, fiercely, and Han turns her face to the fire.

* * *

Elder Gu dies on the fortieth night, at the turn of the watch, with Wenyuan's hand in his.

It is quiet. It is nothing like what Han feared. The tower is dim, the lamp low; the wind has dropped, and the snow falls straight down past the window. Gu sits on his stool, small and wasted, with the pale glow almost gone. Wenyuan kneels beside him, in plain gray, with his sword laid across the floor. Qinghe stands behind him with her hands folded. Han stands at the door.

"You are certain?" says the old man.

"I am."

"It will not be pleasant."

"I have been told."

"You may change your mind. Until the last breath. The stone does not mind."

"I will not change it," says Wenyuan.

Gu smiles, a thin dry smile, the smile of a man who has won an argument and is too tired to enjoy it. He takes Wenyuan's hand in both of his, and the glow that had been fading rises one last time, bright and white, like a lamp fanned by a breath. It runs up the Elder's arms and down into the younger man's. Wenyuan gasps. His back arches. For one long, bright moment the tower is full of light.

Then it goes out.

Gu's hands fall open. His eyes are closed. His chest does not rise. Wenyuan kneels there with his head bowed, swaying, and a faint pale glow now burning in his own skin, in the lines of his face, in the whites of his eyes, and the whole of section nine seems to sigh around them, a long low settling of stone on stone.

"He is gone," says Qinghe.

"Yes."

"And you?"

Wenyuan lifts his head. His eyes have gone the color of moonlight. He looks at his wife, and his face is the same face, broad and plain and tired. But there is something under it that was not there before, a vast slow patience, like the patience of a mountain.

"I can feel it," he says. "The whole Wall. Every stone. I can feel a mouse in the lower gate."

"Is it heavy?"

"No." He considers. "It is like being very large and very still. It is not unpleasant."

"And your feet?"

He glances down. He moves his toes. They do not move.

"Gone," he says mildly. "Already. I had been told."

Qinghe makes a sound in her throat. She goes down on her knees in front of him and takes his dead feet in her hands, in their gray wool socks, and holds them, and bows her head.

Han turns away. She walks to the window, and stands with her forehead against the cold glass, and watches the snow come down on the Wall. On the parapet below her, the sentry has begun to sing. It is a low slow tune, the kind that is sung over the dead. One by one, along the length of the rampart, the others take it up, until the whole two miles is humming with it, and she cannot tell which of the voices are men and which are stone.
